rationale: Receipt 149052bc9a0d495985d41bd165deada3 confirms the predicted fan-out skew: with decided 10, compacted 5, a trailing cursor at 1 and a fast cursor at 6, the fast subscriber's stream is 10,8,9,10 while the slow subscriber's is T5,6,7,8,9,10,8,9,10. A lagging peer therefore causes another subscriber to receive entry 10 where it expected entry 7, skipping 7-9 and duplicating 10. This update records the executed consequence and restates the decided-subscription account for this experiment.

knowledge.statement: On the executed ten-entry, trim-to-five run, simulating the actor's fan-out with a trailing cursor at 1 and a fast cursor at 6 produced slow_stream T5,6,7,8,9,10,8,9,10 and fast_stream 10,8,9,10: the fast subscriber received entry 10 for the position where it expected the entry after cursor 6 (entry 7), then 8,9,10, so entries 7,8,9 were never delivered in order and entry 10 was delivered twice.
knowledge.conditions: Five OmniPaxos instances, ten decided entries, trim to 5, MemoryStorage, unit batch; two cursors simulated over real read_decided_suffix outputs with the actor's push_to_all_subs rule (min_next = min cursor, start = cursor - min_next, one cursor step per element). Channels and backpressure are not simulated.

interpretations.rationale: This experiment shows the fan-out consequence of the decided-stream defect and extends the earlier single-subscriber witness, which remains in its own interpretation. Receipt 149052bc9a0d495985d41bd165deada3 ran fanout_skips_entries_for_fast_subscriber_with_lagging_peer (exit 0, test passed); its declared comparison (fast_stream eq 10,8,9,10) is complete and holds, evaluating event 1. Event 0 fixes the setup: decided 10, compacted 5, trailing cursor 1, fast cursor 6. Event 1 reports slow_stream T5,6,7,8,9,10,8,9,10 and fast_stream 10,8,9,10 with both cursors ending at 10. The slow subscriber re-receives 8,9,10 because its cursor advanced one step per element while the marker stood for indices 1-4. The fast subscriber is worse: push_to_all_subs reads from the trailing cursor 1, so the collapsed marker shifts every later element by compacted-1-min_next = 3 positions, and start = 6-1 = 5 lands on the last element, entry 10. The fast subscriber therefore receives entry 10 where it expected entry 7, then receives 8,9,10 on the next round; entry 7 is never delivered and entry 10 is delivered twice. Because the actor treats each pushed element as one committed log position, a single lagging subscriber silently corrupts the decided stream of every other subscriber. The root cause is the same as the earlier witness: the core read collapses a trimmed prefix into one element while the actor advances cursors and offsets fan-out by log index. A subscriber stream that silently omits a committed entry is a stronger violation of the documented in-order decided stream than duplicate delivery, and an application applying entries from the stream would miss entry 7 permanently.
counterevidence: If every cursor is at or above the compacted index, read_decided_suffix returns one element per index and both start and cursor advance are aligned.
If the trailing cursor is exactly compacted - 1, the collapsed marker replaces exactly one index and the offset is zero, so no skew occurs in that round.
The value at any index is unchanged and the recipient could re-read the log itself; the defect is in the delivered stream contract.
The earlier single-subscriber witness is independent evidence for the same root cause and is retained separately.
limitations: Cursors and channel sends are simulated over real core reads; no real subscriber backpressure, capacity limit or actor execution is exercised (omnipaxos_runtime is not a dev-dependency of the test target).
One compaction point, memory storage, unit batch, five instances and no snapshots; snapshot-based compaction produces a Snapshotted element under the same collapse but was not executed.
Exactly two subscribers and three fan-out rounds are simulated; longer runs would continue accumulating the offset.
